breakfast.name: Bouillie de Mil (Millet Porridge)
instructions: Boil water
Stir in millet flour
Cook until thick
Serve with sugar and milk
breakfast.description: Warm millet porridge — Malian morning staple.

breakfast.name: Dégué (Millet Yogurt)
instructions: Steam millet couscous
Mix with yogurt, sugar, vanilla
Serve cold or warm

breakfast.name: Bouillie de Mil (Millet Porridge)
instructions: Bring water to boil
Whisk in millet flour — stir continuously to avoid lumps
Cook 15-20 minutes over medium heat — the porridge thickens
Add milk or evaporated milk — it enriches and smooths
Add sugar, optional cinnamon or vanilla
The consistency should be pourable but thick enough to coat a spoon
Bouillie de mil is Mali's morning staple — millet porridge consumed across the Sahel
Millet is the ancient Sahelian grain — drought-resistant, more nutritious than maize
Before corn arrived from the Americas, millet porridge fed West Africa's empires
The Mali Empire (13th-17th century) was fueled by millet
breakfast.description: Mali's morning millet porridge — ground millet simmered with water and enriched with milk and sugar. Millet is the ancient Sahelian grain, drought-resistant and nutritious, that sustained West Africa's great empires (including the Mali Empire of Mansa Musa). This porridge is older than any other staple in the region.

breakfast.name: Café Touba (Sacred Spiced Coffee)
ingredients: Selim pepper (Djar — the sacred West African spice)
instructions: Café Touba uses the Selim pepper (also called Guinea pepper or Djar) — a long, aromatic West African spice
Grind coffee with crushed Selim pepper — the pepper is added before grinding
Brew as black coffee — filter or pour-over
The Selim pepper gives a warm, resinous, slightly peppery-spicy note distinct from regular coffee
Add sugar — Café Touba is typically drunk sweet
Café Touba originates from the holy city of Touba (Senegal) but spread across West Africa
In Mali it's a standard street coffee sold from vendors with thermoses
The sacred association: Mouride brotherhood considers Café Touba spiritually blessed
The spiced coffee is drunk every morning by millions across the Sahel
breakfast.description: Mali's sacred spiced coffee — coffee ground with Selim pepper (Djar), a West African spice with a warm, resinous quality unlike black pepper. Originated in the holy city of Touba and spread as a sacred Mouride Brotherhood beverage. Drunk sweet every morning, sold from thermoses by street vendors. The Selim pepper fragrance is instantly recognizable as West Africa.

lunch.name: Tigadegena (Peanut Stew)
instructions: Brown meat
Sauté onion, garlic, tomatoes
Add peanut paste and water
Return meat, simmer 30 min
Add okra, cook 10 min
Serve with rice
lunch.description: Mali's national dish — thick peanut stew with meat.

lunch.name: Riz au Gras (Fatty Rice)
instructions: Brown beef, sauté vegetables
Add tomato paste and rice
Cook covered until done
lunch.description: One-pot rice with meat and vegetables.

lunch.name: Domoda (Peanut Stew)
instructions: Fry onion, garlic in oil
Add meat — brown slightly
Add tomato paste and fresh tomato — cook down
Add water
Add ground peanuts or peanut butter — stir until dissolved into the sauce
Simmer 25-30 minutes — the peanut sauce thickens as it cooks
Season with salt, chili
Domoda is Mali's peanut stew — shared with Gambia, Senegal under different names
The peanut is West Africa's most important flavor element
Groundnut cultivation spread across the Sahel as an economic crop in the 19th-20th century
The rich, thick peanut-tomato stew is deeply satisfying over rice or millet
lunch.description: Mali's peanut stew — meat braised in a thick sauce of ground peanuts, tomato, and onion. West Africa's peanut stew appears under different names (domoda, mafé, groundnut soup) from Gambia to Nigeria; Mali's version is rich and thick with tomato. The peanut is West Africa's most important flavor foundation.

lunch.name: Dibi (Grilled Meat)
ingredients: Lamb or goat (bone-in cuts — ribs, shoulder)
instructions: Dibi is the West African grilled meat — simplest preparation
Season meat with onion, salt, chili, optional mustard
Grill directly over charcoal — the char is part of the flavor
The fat drips and causes flare-ups — this is intentional
Meat should be charred outside, juicy inside
Serve with onion-mustard-chili sauce on the side
Dibi grills (dibiteries) are found throughout Mali and West Africa
A dibiterie is a charcoal-grill restaurant — lamb or goat over open fire
Dibi is the West African barbecue — the social eating of grilled meat around fire
The simplicity is the point: good meat, fire, onion, salt
lunch.description: Mali's charcoal-grilled lamb — bone-in cuts over an open charcoal fire until charred outside and juicy inside, served with an onion-mustard-chili sauce. Dibiteries (dibi grills) are everywhere in Mali and West Africa. The social ritual of eating grilled meat directly from the fire, standing around the grill, is West Africa's barbecue culture.

dinner.name: Tô (Millet Paste)
instructions: Boil water, stir in flour
Cook until very thick
Shape into smooth dome
Serve with okra or peanut sauce
dinner.description: Dense millet paste — eaten with sauce.

dinner.name: Fakoye (Okra Sauce)
instructions: Sauté onion in palm oil
Add sliced okra, cook until slimy
Add fish and dawadawa
Simmer 15 min
Serve with tô or rice
dinner.description: Thick okra sauce with dried fish.

dinner.name: Maafe (Peanut Butter Stew Variant)
ingredients: Bitter tomato (optional — the African bitter tomato, ntomo)
instructions: Maafe is closely related to domoda — both are peanut stews
The distinction: maafe often includes root vegetables (sweet potato, carrot)
Brown meat with onion, garlic
Add tomato paste, peanut butter, water — create the sauce
Add vegetables — sweet potato adds sweetness against the savory peanut
Optional: bitter tomato (ntomo) — a small, bitter African eggplant variety that adds complexity
Simmer until meat is tender and vegetables cooked
Season, adjust peanut richness
Maafe is the Bambara people's dish — Mali's largest ethnic group
The Bambara version often includes bitter tomato for complexity
Served over white rice or tô (maize porridge)
dinner.description: Mali's Bambara peanut stew — meat and optional sweet potato braised in a peanut butter-tomato sauce, sometimes with bitter tomato (ntomo, an African eggplant) for complexity. The Bambara people are Mali's largest ethnic group; maafe is their foundational dish. The bitterness of ntomo against the peanut richness is a distinctly Bambara flavor balance.

dinner.name: Poulet Yassa (Onion-Marinated Chicken)
ingredients: Onions (enormous quantity — 4-5 large onions per chicken)
instructions: Yassa marinade: quarter all onions, mix with lemon juice, mustard, oil, garlic, salt, pepper, chili
The amount of onion is extreme — more onion than seems reasonable
Marinate chicken in yassa marinade at least 2 hours (overnight is better)
The lemon and mustard tenderize the chicken
Remove chicken from marinade — grill or fry until browned
Set aside the marinated onions — fry them down in oil until very soft and caramelized (30 minutes)
The onion mass reduces dramatically — they become sweet, tangy, golden
Add chicken back into the caramelized onions
Braise briefly to combine
Poulet yassa originates in Senegal/Casamance but is widespread across West Africa
The extreme onion-lemon-mustard combination is unlike any other West African dish
dinner.description: Mali's adopted Senegalese masterpiece — chicken marinated for hours in an extreme quantity of lemon juice, mustard, and onion, then grilled and returned to the caramelized marinade onions. The sheer volume of onion (reduced to a sweet, tangy mass) is the shock and the magic. Yassa originated in Senegal's Casamance region but spread across the Sahel.

snacks.name: Fataya (Fried Pastries)
ingredients: Filling: ground beef, onion, egg, parsley
instructions: Make dough, cut circles
Fill with meat mixture
Fold, seal edges
Deep fry until golden

snacks.name: Brochettes (Meat Skewers)
instructions: Cube meat into small pieces
Season with crushed Maggi, chili, onion, salt
Thread onto small skewers — often multiple small skewers sold together
Grill over charcoal — they cook quickly, small cubes
The Maggi cube is West Africa's universal umami addition — widely used across the Sahel
Brochettes are sold at night markets, bus stations, and roadside
Eaten walking, as a snack between meals
The Maggi-seasoned grilled meat smell is West Africa's night market signature
Brochettes in Mali are smaller and simpler than formal dibi — a quick snack format
snacks.description: Mali's street skewer — small meat cubes seasoned with Maggi seasoning and chili, grilled quickly over charcoal. The Maggi cube is West Africa's universal seasoning — present in virtually every Sahelian street food context. Sold at night markets and bus stations, eaten walking. The Maggi-grilled meat fragrance is West Africa's street food signature.

snacks.name: Alloco (Fried Plantain)
instructions: Peel plantains at the ripe yellow-black stage — the sweetness is maximum at this point
Slice diagonally into thick rounds
Fry in hot oil until golden and caramelized on both sides
The natural sugars caramelize — slight crispiness outside, soft and sweet inside
Season with salt
Serve with chili sauce (piment) on the side
The sweet-salt-heat combination is the alloco experience
Alloco is West Africa's universal plantain snack — Ivory Coast, Ghana, Mali
In Mali it's sold from roadside fryers alongside grilled meat
The sweet, caramelized plantain against the spicy piment is addictive
snacks.description: Mali's fried sweet plantain — ripe yellow-black plantains sliced and fried until caramelized, served with chili sauce. The sweet-salt-heat combination is the alloco experience. Alloco is universal across West Africa (Ivory Coast, Ghana, Mali) — the ripe plantain's caramelizing sugars create a natural sweetness no added sugar could improve.

snacks.name: Bissap Jelly (Hibiscus Candy)
instructions: Steep hibiscus flowers in hot water — the liquid turns deep red-purple immediately
Strain and sweeten generously
Add agar agar or gelatin — the bissap gels beautifully
Pour into molds or a flat tray — the color is extraordinary
Refrigerate until set
Cut into pieces
The hibiscus gel has a tart-sweet flavor and the striking magenta color
Bissap hibiscus is the most-consumed drink in Mali and West Africa
The candy version puts the same flavor in a solid, transportable form
The intense color from hibiscus anthocyanins is natural — no artificial coloring
snacks.description: Mali's hibiscus candy — the famous bissap (hibiscus) drink set into a gel with agar agar, producing an intensely magenta, tart-sweet candy. The magenta color from hibiscus anthocyanins needs no artificial enhancement. Bissap is West Africa's most consumed soft drink; this candy form is the same flavor made portable and solid.

snacks.name: Tô (Millet or Maize Porridge Ball)
instructions: Tô is the Bambara people's staple — a stiff porridge formed into a ball or firm mound
Boil water, add flour gradually — stir vigorously
Cook until very thick — much thicker than porridge
The consistency should hold its shape when scooped with a spoon
Tô is not eaten with utensils — a piece is torn off and rolled in the fingers
This ball is then dipped into the relish (sauce, stew)
The tô itself is bland — the sauce is the flavor
Tô is snack-sized when made for individual portions
The neutral flavor is intentional — it's a vehicle for whatever sauce accompanies it
In rural Mali, tô and sauce is the daily meal
snacks.description: Mali's Bambara staple — extremely thick millet or maize porridge cooked until stiff enough to hold its shape, torn by hand and dipped in sauce. Tô has no flavor of its own; it is a vehicle. The sauce (peanut, meat, or vegetable) is where all flavor lives. In rural Mali, tô with sauce is eaten at least once daily.

desserts.name: Ngomi (Sweet Millet Balls)
instructions: Mix millet flour with peanut paste and honey
Shape into small balls
Serve as is

desserts.name: Naan Pains (Fried Wheat Balls)
instructions: Mix flour, sugar, yeast, water into a soft dough
Add cardamom if using
Let rise 30-45 minutes
Fry spoonfuls in hot oil — they puff and brown
Drain and eat warm
Naan pains are Mali's street sweet — small fried dough balls
Sold at morning markets and in the evening
The name 'naan pains' is a West African linguistic blend (French 'pain' + Arabic/Indian 'naan')
Simple, sweet, affordable
The yeast puff and the sugary dough is a universal human pleasure in Sahelian form
desserts.description: Mali's fried sweet dough balls — a yeasted dough with sugar and optional cardamom, fried until puffed and golden. The name blends French 'pain' (bread) with the Arabic-Indian 'naan' — a Sahelian linguistic fusion. Sold at morning markets and evening stalls, they're affordable sweetness on Mali's streets.

desserts.name: Dégué (Millet-Yogurt Dessert)
ingredients: Fermented millet (fonio or small millet balls — cooked)
instructions: Cook small millet balls (soaked millet that has been shaped and dried)
Cool completely
Mix with yogurt or soured milk — generous amount
Add sugar, optional condensed milk for richness
Dégué is cool and tangy — perfect for Mali's heat
The fermented milk against the neutral millet creates a satisfying sweet-sour combination
Dégué is served at celebrations and as a daily dessert or snack
The creamy, slightly tangy yogurt with the grainy millet texture is the combination
Also popular in Senegal, Mauritania — a Sahelian dessert tradition
The temperature contrast (cool, refreshing) is important in West Africa's heat
desserts.description: Mali's millet-yogurt dessert — cooked millet balls mixed with soured milk or yogurt and sugar, served cool. The neutral millet grain against the tangy fermented milk creates a satisfying textural and flavor contrast. Cool and refreshing in West Africa's heat, dégué is both celebration food and daily dessert throughout the Sahel.

drinks.name: Dabileni (Hibiscus Drink)
instructions: Boil hibiscus and ginger 10 min
Strain, add sugar and mint
Chill

drinks.name: Dolo (Millet Beer)
instructions: Sprout millet grains
Cook mash
Ferment 3-5 days
Strain, serve at room temperature
drinks.description: Traditional millet beer — social and ceremonial.

drinks.name: Bissap (Hibiscus Drink)
instructions: Rinse hibiscus calyces briefly
Steep in hot water 10-15 minutes — the water turns deep crimson immediately
The longer the steep, the more tart
Strain out the calyces
Add generous sugar — bissap is drunk sweet
Optional: add fresh ginger (popular combination), mint, orange blossom water
Serve chilled with lots of ice
Bissap is the most consumed drink in Mali and across West Africa
The deep red-purple color is extraordinary — entirely natural from hibiscus anthocyanins
The tartness is like cranberry — very refreshing in heat
Also popular in the Caribbean and Latin America (agua de Jamaica)
drinks.description: Mali's national drink — hibiscus flowers steeped into a deep crimson, tart-sweet drink, served chilled. The extraordinary color is natural (hibiscus anthocyanins). Consumed more than any other drink in Mali and across West Africa. Also known as agua de Jamaica in Latin America (where African diaspora brought it). The tartness in heat is one of the world's most refreshing flavors.
